title: Defining the Question and Planning the Workflow

steps.title: From Vague Complaint to Scoped Business Question
steps.lede: The operations team at QuickShip says deliveries feel slow lately. That is not yet something you can analyze.

blocks.text: Before any analytical work begins, the question to be addressed, its context, and its boundaries should be identified. Turning a vague complaint into a workable target is called scoping. Scoping ensures an appropriate, common understanding of the problem is defined, and that expectations are aligned with what the analysis can produce.

steps.title: Why Every Later Step Depends on the Scoped Question
steps.lede: Every later capstone step — what data to retrieve, how to clean it, what to compute — serves this one sentence.

blocks.text: For QuickShip, scoping the vague complaint means settling its context and boundaries: which orders (a specific quarter's deliveries), which measure (delivery time against a target), and which unit of comparison (delivery zone). The result is a specific business question: 'Which delivery zones are missing the delivery-time target, and by how much, over the last quarter?' Scope it loosely, and the rest of the project has nothing precise to aim at.

steps.title: Scoping the Question
steps.lede: The operations team says 'deliveries feel slow lately.' Which of the following is the best scoped business question?

public.prompt: The QuickShip operations team says: 'Deliveries feel slow lately — can you look into it?' Which of the following is a correctly scoped business question?

options.text: Which delivery zones are missing the 25-minute target, and by how much, over the last quarter?
What is happening with QuickShip's operations?

opt_scoped.message: Correct. This question names the context (last quarter's orders), the measure (delivery time vs. the 25-minute target), and the unit of comparison (delivery zones) — all three elements of a properly scoped business question.

opt_vague.message: This is still vague — it does not identify the context (which orders, which time period), the measure (delivery time vs. what target?), or the unit of comparison (which zones or cities?). Scoping requires all three.

opt_too_broad.message: This is too broad to be analytical. A scoped business question must identify the context, the measure, and the unit of comparison — not just name the company and a vague area of concern.

opt_solution.message: This jumps to a solution before the analysis is done. A scoped business question identifies what the analysis will measure and compare — it does not pre-suppose the answer.

correct.message: Right. A scoped business question identifies the context, the measure, and the unit of comparison — so the analyst and the stakeholder share the same understanding of what the analysis will and will not answer.

incorrect.message: A scoped business question must name: (1) the context (which data, which time period), (2) the measure (what is being compared), and (3) the unit of comparison (zones, cities, etc.).

hints: Does the question name a specific time period and dataset?
Does the question name a specific measure (e.g. delivery time vs. a target) and a unit of comparison (e.g. zones)?

steps.title: Write Your Scoped Business Question
steps.lede: Using the QuickShip scenario, write the scoped business question in one sentence. Include the context (which orders), the measure (what you will compare), and the boundary (what the analysis will and will not answer).

public.instruction: Write a one-sentence business question for a capstone dataset of your choice. Your question must identify: (1) the context — what data and what time period or scope; (2) the boundaries — what measure and unit of comparison the analysis will address. Use the QuickShip example as a model: 'Which delivery zones are missing the 25-minute target, and by how much, over the last quarter?'
checklist: The question names a specific dataset or data source.
The question names a specific time period or scope.
The question names a specific measure (what is being compared or evaluated).
The question names a unit of comparison (e.g. zones, cities, products).
The question makes clear what the analysis will and will not answer.

rubric.criterion: Names a specific measurable question with context and boundaries.
States the context (what data, what time period or scope).
States the boundaries (what measure and unit of comparison).
Makes clear what the analysis will and will not answer.

correct.message: Well done. Your scoped question names the context and boundaries, so the analyst and stakeholder share the same understanding of what the analysis will and will not answer.

incorrect.message: Check your question against the checklist: does it name the data, the time period, the measure, and the unit of comparison? A vague question cannot guide the rest of the analysis.

hints: Start with: 'Which [unit of comparison] are [measure] [condition], over [time period]?'
The QuickShip example names zones, delivery time vs. target, and last quarter — use that as a template.

steps.title: Matching Each Data Source to Its Retrieval Tool
steps.lede: With the question scoped, the next decision is how to get the data. QuickShip's order records live in a SQL database; the driver roster is kept in an Excel workbook.

blocks.text: Data that lives in a SQL database can be retrieved with a SQL query; pandas' SQL query wrappers (pandas.io.sql) facilitate this retrieval. So the orders table, sitting in the company's database, is a SQL-query job.

read_excel() reads an Excel file directly into a DataFrame. So the driver roster workbook, which never touches a database, is a read_excel() job instead. The capstone ends up using both: a SQL query pulls the last quarter's orders (zone, driver_id, delivery_time_min) from the orders table, and read_excel() pulls the driver roster (driver_id, name, zone, shift) from the spreadsheet.

steps.title: Which Tool for Which Source?
steps.lede: QuickShip's driver roster is stored in an Excel workbook. Which retrieval method should you use?

public.prompt: The QuickShip capstone has two data sources: (A) an orders table in a SQL relational database, and (B) a driver roster saved as an Excel workbook. Which retrieval methods are correct?

options.text: A: SQL query via pandas.io.sql; B: read_excel().
A: SQL query via pandas.io.sql; B: SQL query via pandas.io.sql.
A: read_excel(); B: SQL query via pandas.io.sql.

opt_correct.message: Correct. Data in a SQL database is retrieved with a SQL query via pandas.io.sql. An Excel workbook is read directly into a DataFrame with read_excel(). The retrieval method follows the source.

opt_both_sql.message: SQL queries work for SQL databases, but not for Excel workbooks. An Excel workbook is read with read_excel(), not a SQL query.

opt_both_excel.message: read_excel() reads Excel files, not SQL databases. Data in a SQL database is retrieved with a SQL query via pandas.io.sql.

opt_swapped.message: The methods are swapped. read_excel() reads Excel files; SQL queries via pandas.io.sql retrieve data from SQL databases. The retrieval method must match where the data lives.

correct.message: Right. The retrieval method follows the source: SQL query for the database, read_excel() for the workbook.

incorrect.message: Match the retrieval method to where the data lives: SQL databases use SQL queries via pandas.io.sql; Excel workbooks use read_excel().

hints: Where does each data source live — in a database or in a file?
pandas.io.sql is for SQL databases; read_excel() is for Excel files.

steps.title: The Six-Stage Analytical Workflow
steps.lede: With the question scoped and both retrieval tools chosen, sketch the whole project's shape before touching either one.

blocks.text: An analytical project is commonly structured through phases that begin with scoping the question and end with delivering and communicating the results. A phase such as scoping may need to be revisited if a later phase encounters changes or limitations — for example, if cleaning the orders data reveals that 'last quarter' is ambiguous in the source system, that sends you back to re-scope rather than pressing on.

Within that structure, the source data is retrieved (via a SQL query or a spreadsheet import), and data quality should be assessed at every stage, with quality improvements such as cleaning focused as early as possible. So right after the orders query and the roster import, the capstone checks for problems like missing delivery times — rather than waiting until the final analysis to discover them.

steps.title: Modeling Multi-Table Data and Communicating Results
steps.lede: Two stages of the workflow deserve special attention: modeling (when data spans more than one table) and delivery.

blocks.text: Where the project's data spans more than one table, the modeling stage connects related tables; relationships are what connect related information between tables. The capstone's orders and drivers are two such tables, so a modeling stage links them — using driver_id as the join key — before any deeper analysis relies on both together.

In the delivery and communication stage, insights are communicated to the commissioner and approver — the people who need them. Activities may include producing summary packs and reports, launching dashboards or websites, and presentations. The capstone's version of this is reporting the zone-delay findings back to the operations team that raised the original complaint.

steps.title: Workflow Stage Order
steps.lede: Which of the following correctly describes the order of the first three stages in the QuickShip capstone workflow?

public.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes the order of the first three stages in the QuickShip capstone workflow?

opt_correct.message: Correct. The workflow begins with scoping the question, then retrieving the source data, then cleaning and modeling it. Quality is assessed at every stage, with cleaning focused as early as possible.

opt_retrieve_first.message: Retrieving data before scoping the question means you do not yet know what data you need. Scoping comes first — it defines the question, context, and boundaries that guide every later stage.

opt_analyze_early.message: You cannot analyze data before retrieving it. The correct order is Scope → Retrieve → Clean/Model → Analyze. Scoping defines the question; retrieval brings in the data; cleaning prepares it for analysis.

opt_clean_first.message: You cannot clean data before scoping the question or retrieving the data. The workflow must start with scoping, then retrieval, then cleaning.

correct.message: Right. Scope → Retrieve → Clean/Model are the first three stages. Scoping defines the question; retrieval brings in the data; cleaning prepares it for analysis.

incorrect.message: The workflow must start with scoping the question — you cannot retrieve or clean data before you know what question you are answering.

hints: Which stage defines the question, context, and boundaries that guide everything else?
You cannot retrieve data before you know what question you are answering.

steps.title: When to Revisit an Earlier Stage
steps.lede: During the cleaning stage, you discover that 'last quarter' is ambiguous in the orders database. What should you do?

public.prompt: During the cleaning stage, you discover that 'last quarter' is ambiguous in the orders database — it could mean the calendar quarter or the fiscal quarter. What should you do?

options.text: Revisit the scoping stage to clarify the time-period boundary with the operations team before continuing.
Pick one interpretation and proceed — the analysis will be the same either way.
Skip the ambiguous rows and continue with the data that is clearly within the quarter.
Run the analysis twice — once for each interpretation — and present both results.

opt_revisit_scope.message: Correct. A phase such as scoping may need to be revisited if a later phase encounters changes or limitations. An ambiguous time-period boundary is a scoping issue — it must be resolved with the stakeholder before the analysis can proceed correctly.

opt_pick_one.message: Picking an interpretation without checking with the stakeholder risks answering the wrong question. The scoping stage established the boundaries of the analysis — an ambiguity there must be resolved by revisiting scoping.

opt_skip.message: Skipping ambiguous rows changes the scope of the analysis without the stakeholder's knowledge. The correct action is to revisit the scoping stage and clarify the boundary with the operations team.

opt_both.message: Running the analysis twice without resolving the ambiguity leaves the stakeholder to choose between two results they did not ask for. The correct action is to revisit scoping and agree on the correct time-period boundary.

correct.message: Right. A later phase discovering an ambiguity in the original question is exactly when scoping must be revisited. The workflow is not strictly linear — earlier phases can be returned to when needed.

incorrect.message: An ambiguity in the time-period boundary is a scoping issue. The correct action is to revisit the scoping stage and clarify with the stakeholder — not to pick an interpretation unilaterally.

hints: Which stage established the time-period boundary for the analysis?
The workflow allows earlier phases to be revisited when a later phase encounters a limitation.

steps.title: What You Learned
steps.lede: Three foundations every remaining capstone step builds on.

blocks.text: Scoping converts a vague complaint into a specific question with context and boundaries. The retrieval method follows the source: SQL query for the database, read_excel() for the workbook. The workflow runs Scope → Retrieve → Clean/Model → Analyze → Visualize → Communicate, with quality checked throughout and stages such as scoping open to revisiting.

remediation_steps.title: Scoping: Context and Boundaries
remediation_steps.lede: A scoped question has three parts: what you will measure, which records you will use, and what the analysis will not answer.

blocks.text: Before any analytical work begins, the question to be addressed, its context, and its boundaries should be identified. For QuickShip, the context is last quarter's orders and the boundary is delivery time by zone — not every possible cause of delay. Scoping ensures you and the operations team share the same understanding of what the analysis will and will not answer.

remediation_steps.title: Source Determines Tool
remediation_steps.lede: The retrieval method is not a preference — it follows where the data actually lives.

blocks.text: Data that lives in a SQL database is retrieved with a SQL query via pandas.io.sql. Data stored in an Excel workbook is read with read_excel(). For QuickShip: the orders table lives in the company's database (SQL query), and the driver roster is an Excel workbook (read_excel()). Matching each source to its tool is the first executable step of the workflow.

remediation_steps.title: The Workflow Is Not a Straight Line
remediation_steps.lede: Any stage can send you back to an earlier one — that is a feature, not a failure.

blocks.text: An analytical project commonly runs Scope → Retrieve → Clean/Model → Analyze → Visualize → Communicate. But a phase such as scoping may need to be revisited if a later phase encounters changes or limitations. If cleaning the orders data reveals that 'last quarter' is ambiguous in the source system, that sends you back to re-scope the question rather than pressing on with a flawed definition.
